extracted.intended_audience: editors, publishers, journal owners, peer reviewers, and authors involved in medical journal publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and recommendations for conduct, reporting, editing, and publication in medical journals, covering editorial freedom, peer review, corrections, misconduct, copyright, overlapping publication, preprints, supplements, electronic publishing, advertising, and media interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer timeliness and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are expected to respond promptly to requests to review and to submit reviews within the time agreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should accept or decline review invitations promptly and adhere to agreed deadlines to facilitate timely editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conduct and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers’ comments should be constructive, honest, and polite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should focus on improving manuscripts, avoid personal attacks, and be communicated respectfully to authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conflict of interest disclosure and recusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should declare their relationships and activities that might bias their evaluation of a manuscript and recuse themselves from the peer-review process if a conflict exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must disclose relevant financial and non-financial relationships; when conflicts are present they should decline review or be excluded to preserve impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer use of AI tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be aware that AI can generate authoritative-sounding output that can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution when using or relying on AI-generated material in reviews; verify facts and do not treat AI output as authoritative without independent validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal ownership transparency and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: A medical journal should explicitly state its governance and relationship to a journal owner (e.g., a sponsoring society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should make clear who owns or sponsors them and how governance is structured so readers and contributors understand any potential influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal owners’ responsibility to reduce carbon emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, publishers, journal owners, and other stakeholders should work together to develop immediate strategies to reduce carbon emissions, with a goal toward achieving net zero carbon emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners and stakeholders should adopt and pursue concrete policies to limit the carbon footprint of publishing activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment, contract, and dismissal of editors by owners
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the responsibility of medical journal owners to appoint and dismiss editors. Owners should provide editors at the time of their appointment with a contract that clearly states their rights and duties, authority, the general terms of their appointment, and mechanisms for resolving conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor contracts should define expectations and authorities; dismissals should be for substantial reasons (e.g., scientific misconduct, disagreement over long-term editorial direction, inadequate performance, inappropriate behavior) and follow fair procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent evaluation for appointments and dismissals
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments and dismissals should be based on evaluations by a panel of independent experts, rather than by a small number of executives of the owning organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent panels to protect editorial independence and to provide fair, expert assessment, especially for contentious dismissals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial freedom (definition and protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors-in-chief have full authority over the entire editorial content of their journal and the timing of publication of that content; journal owners should not interfere in the evaluation, selection, scheduling, or editing of individual articles either directly or by creating an environment that strongly influences decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions should be based on validity and importance to readers, not commercial implications; editors should be free to express critical but responsible views without fear of retribution; editors should have direct access to the highest level of ownership; owners should not exert undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors’ authority over advertising and journal brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors-in-chief should also have the final say in decisions about which advertisements or sponsored content, including supplements, the journal will and will not carry, and they should have final say in use of the journal brand and in overall policy regarding commercial use of journal content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should make final decisions on advertising and sponsored material to prevent commercial influence over editorial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for editorial decisions and legal protection
rubrics_metrics.description: To support editorial decisions and potentially controversial expressions of opinion, owners should ensure that appropriate insurance is obtained in the event of legal action against the editors, and should ensure that legal advice is available when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners should provide legal resources and insurance so editors can defend editorial freedom and responsible expression without undue personal or institutional risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial advisory boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals are encouraged to establish an independent and diverse editorial advisory board to help the editor establish and maintain editorial policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisory boards can provide breadth of expertise and support for editorial policies and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors’ responsibility for fact-checking and journalistic practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should take all reasonable steps to check the facts in journal commentary, including that in news sections and social media postings, and should ensure that staff working for the journal adhere to best journalistic practices including contemporaneous note-taking and seeking a response from all parties when possible before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply rigorous fact-checking for commentary and news; maintain contemporaneous records and seek responses to avoid libel and protect public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of authors and peer reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should defend the confidentiality of authors and peer reviewers (names and reviewer comments) in accordance with ICMJE policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect identities and reviewer reports as required by policy, releasing information only in accordance with stated procedures and legal/ethical obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics approval for human research (Helsinki Declaration)
rubrics_metrics.description: All investigators should ensure that the planning, conduct, and reporting of human research are in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration as revised in 2024. All authors should seek approval to conduct research from an independent local, regional, or national review body and be prepared to provide documentation when requested by editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If doubt exists whether the research complies with Helsinki, authors must explain the rationale and demonstrate explicit approval of doubtful aspects by a review body; institutional approval does not preclude editorial judgment about appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of patient privacy and informed consent for identifiable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients have a right to privacy that should not be violated without informed consent. Identifying information, including names, initials, or hospital numbers, should not be published in written descriptions, photographs, or pedigrees unless essential for scientific purposes and the patient (or parent or guardian) gives written informed consent for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informed consent requires that an identifiable patient be shown the manuscript to be published; authors should disclose whether identifiable material might be available via the Internet; consent should be written and archived with the journal, authors, or both as dictated by local regulations; journals should state consent requirements in instructions for authors and indicate when consent was obtained in published articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission and deidentification of nonessential identifying details
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonessential identifying details should be omitted. Informed consent should be obtained if there is any doubt that anonymity can be maintained. Masking the eye region in photographs of patients is inadequate protection of anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and editors should assure that deidentification does not distort scientific meaning and should note such assurance in the publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal research reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting experiments on animals, authors should indicate whether institutional and national standards for the care and use of laboratory animals were followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State compliance with relevant animal welfare standards and approvals in the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and minimum standards for issuing corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: If a correction is needed, journals should publish a correction notice as soon as possible detailing changes from and citing the original publication; the correction should be on an electronic or numbered print page that is included in an electronic or a print Table of Contents to ensure proper indexing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also post a new article version with details of the changes and dates; archive all prior versions (directly accessible or available on request); previous electronic versions should prominently note that there are more recent versions; citations should point to the most recent version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling pervasive errors and retraction with republication
rubrics_metrics.description: Pervasive errors from coding problems or miscalculations may require corrections; errors serious enough to invalidate a paper’s results and conclusions may require retraction. Retraction with republication can be considered in cases where honest error leads to major change but the underlying science appears valid and the changed version survives further review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When republishing, explain changes and show their extent (supplement or appendix) for transparency; older papers may be harder to correct and editors may reasonably determine correction isn't warranted in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific misconduct definitions and response procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific misconduct includes but is not limited to data fabrication, data falsification (including deceptive manipulation of images), purposeful failure to disclose relationships, and plagiarism. When alleged, editors should initiate appropriate procedures (e.g., COPE guidance), consider informing institutions and funders, and may publish an expression of concern pending outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek the outcome of institutional investigations; if misconduct is proved, publish retraction; expressions of concern and retractions should be prominently labelled, indexed, linked bidirectionally to the original article, and include an explanation and citation; retracted articles should remain public and clearly labelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors’ actions regarding an author's other work after proven misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of previous work by the author of a fraudulent paper cannot be assumed; editors may ask the author's institution to assure them of the validity of other work or may retract it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assurances are not provided, editors may publish announcements expressing concern about the validity of prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and licensing transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should make clear the type of copyright under which work will be published, and if the journal retains copyright, should detail the journal’s position on the transfer of copyright for all types of content, including audio, video, protocols, and data sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether authors must transfer copyright, whether publication licenses are required, and use of Creative Commons or other licenses; note exceptions (e.g., some government employee works) and possibilities for editors to waive copyright on content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on duplicate submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not submit the same manuscript, in the same or different languages, simultaneously to more than one journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate submission risks multiple journals undertaking review/editing of the same manuscript and potential disputes over publication rights; authors who submit simultaneously should expect at least prompt rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate and prior publication policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate publication is publication of a paper that overlaps substantially with one already published without clear, visible reference to the previous publication. Prior publication may include release of information in the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must disclose related prior or simultaneous material in the submission letter and provide copies to help editors decide handling; duplicate publication of original research is particularly problematic because it can double-count data and distort evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint archive selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who wish to make preprints publicly available should choose preprint archives that (a) clearly identify preprints as not peer-reviewed; (b) require authors to document disclosures of interest; (c) require authors to indicate funding sources; (d) have a process for users to notify administrators about concerns (public commenting desirable); (e) maintain metadata and withdrawal notices for withdrawn preprints; and (f) have a mechanism for authors to indicate subsequent journal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting archives with these features maximizes benefits and minimizes harms of preprint dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting manuscripts that are in preprint archives
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should inform a journal if the work submitted has been posted on a preprint server and provide a link to the preprint, whether posting occurs prior to submission or during peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicating the preprint in the manuscript (e.g., introduction) and ensuring preprints are amended to point readers to subsequent versions (responsibility of authors) helps transparency; authors should not post the published article or peer-review interim versions to the preprint archive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing preprints in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: When preprints are cited, the citation should clearly indicate that the reference is a preprint. When a preprint has been subsequently published, authors should cite the published article rather than the preprint when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the word 'preprint' after the citation, provide DOI and link if available, and exercise caution about citing preprints that were posted and never subsequently published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable secondary publication conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary publication of material published elsewhere may be justifiable provided conditions are met: (1) authors have approval from editors of both journals (the secondary editor must have access to the primary version); (2) the priority of the primary publication is respected by a negotiated publication interval; (3) the paper for secondary publication is intended for a different group of readers; (4) the secondary version faithfully reflects the authors, data, and interpretations of the primary version; (5) the secondary version informs readers and cites the primary reference; and (6) the title of the secondary publication should indicate it is a secondary publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary publication is appropriate mainly to disseminate important information to different audiences; NLM does not consider translations as republications for indexing when the original is indexed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscripts based on the same database
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts from separate groups or the same group analyzing the same data set should be considered independently because they may differ in methods or conclusions; if similar, editors may reasonably prefer the manuscript submitted first but may publish more than one if analyses are complementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts should add substantially to each other to warrant separate publication; secondary analyses should cite any primary publication, state that they contain secondary analyses/results, and use the same trial registration number and persistent data set identifier; transparency for planned multiple publications in large trials is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence and post-publication discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical journals should provide readers with a mechanism for submitting comments, questions, or criticisms about published articles (correspondence section or online forum); authors of articles discussed should be asked to respond to substantial criticisms; authors of correspondence should declare competing relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondence may be edited for length and style or left unedited (e.g., online); editors must screen discourteous, inaccurate, or libellous comments; editors may reject irrelevant or uncogent correspondence but should encourage a range of opinions and set time limits to keep debate manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about fees and revenue streams
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should be transparent about their types of revenue streams. Any fees or charges required for manuscript processing and/or publishing materials shall be clearly stated in a place easy for potential authors to find prior to submission or explained before manuscript preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear disclosure of fees helps authors make informed decisions and adheres to principles of transparency and best practice in scholarly publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplements, theme issues, and special series principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplements funded externally or with guest editors should adhere to principles: (1) the journal editor must have full responsibility and control of policies, practices, and content; (2) the editor may appoint external editors and remain responsible; (3) the editor must retain authority to send supplement manuscripts for external peer review and to reject them; (4) the source of the idea and funding and related products should be clearly stated; (5) advertising in supplements should follow the same policies as the primary journal; (6) readers must be able to readily distinguish supplement pages from ordinary editorial pages; (7) journal and supplement editors must not accept personal favors or direct remuneration from sponsors; (8) secondary publication in supplements should be clearly identified by citation of the original paper; and (9) the same authorship and disclosure principles apply to supplements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures protect editorial independence and transparency when external funding or guest editors are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsorships and partnerships governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactions with sponsors, partners, meetings, or other activities should be governed by the same principles outlined for supplements, theme issues, and special series to preserve editorial independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply supplement principles to all external sponsorships and partnerships to prevent undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publishing: linking, versioning, and preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of print and electronic publishing are identical, but electronic publishing raises issues about versioning, link stability, and content preservation. Journals should be cautious about external linking and state that they do not endorse external sites. Permanent preservation of journal articles (on a journal website or in independent archives) is essential; removing an article entirely is almost never justified and if necessary must include a detailed reason and retention in the journal’s internal archive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit content in multiple credible repositories, ensure archives are accessible, transfer files to a responsible third party on journal termination, and post dates for nonarticle web pages updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policy and editor authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should have formal, explicit, written policies for advertising in both print and electronic versions. Best practice prohibits selling advertisements intended to be juxtaposed with editorial content on the same product. Advertisements should be clearly identiﬁable as advertisements and editors should have full and final authority for approving print and online advertisements and for enforcing advertising policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should not carry advertisements for products proven to be seriously harmful to health; enforce applicable regulatory or industry standards; avoid letting advertising influence editorial decisions; consider criticisms of advertisements for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactions with media and embargo systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals’ interactions with media should balance the public’s legitimate interest with the need for vetted peer-reviewed information. An embargo system can help prevent premature media reports and give reporters time to prepare accurate stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may agree with authors not to publicize work while under consideration and with media not to release stories before publication, in return for cooperation (e.g., press releases); embargoes rely on the honor system and can be undermined if not respected by many outlets.
